paragraphs.text: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I is characterized by neonatal renal salt wasting with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis despite elevated aldosterone levels (Geller et al., 1998). The autosomal dominant or sporadic form is milder than the autosomal recessive form and remits with age (Geller et al., 1998; Viemann et al., 2001). Hanukoglu (1991) concluded that type I PHA includes 2 clinically and genetically distinct entities, one with a renal defect and one with defects in multiple target organs.

paragraphs.text: Hanukoglu (1991) studied 2 kindreds with a total of 9 patients with PHA. In kindred I, the proband had renal salt wasting in infancy, with vomiting, failure to thrive, short stature, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, and responded dramatically to a high salt diet (2.5 g/day). Sodium supplementation was stopped at age 2 years. In 7 more family members from 3 generations, clinical expression of PHA ranged from asymptomatic to moderate. In affected members (the proband, mother, and 2 brothers), hyperaldosteronism persisted over 13 years, but plasma renin activity (PRA) fell gradually to near normal values. Hanukoglu (1991) interpreted the persistent hyperaldosteronism with falling PRA as tertiary hyperaldosteronism due to an autonomously functioning zona glomerulosa. In kindred II, the proband, born of a consanguineous marriage, developed severe renal salt loss at age 9 days. She also had increased salivary and sweat electrolytes, consistent with unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids in multiple organs. Life-threatening episodes of salt wasting recurred after age 2 years, and at age 5 years she still needed high-dose salt supplements (14 g/day). A sister died at 9 days of age with PHA symptoms.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) studied 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism: a 28-year-old index case in Melbourne and 2 sibs in Munich, aged 8 and 2 years. The younger Munich sib was less severely affected than his sister. Percoll-separated control monocytes bound [3H]aldosterone with high affinity (Kd approximately 3 nM) and limited capacity (150 to 600 sites per cell). On repeated testing, monocytes from the index case and the older Munich sib showed no [3H]aldosterone binding. The younger sib had 62 sites per cell, more than 2 SD below control values. The parents of the Munich sibs were first cousins and had normal binding. Armanini et al. (1985) concluded that pseudohypoaldosteronism is caused by a defect in the type I (mineralocorticoid) receptor, that the defect may be complete or partial, and that transmission may be autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Sartorato et al. (2003) analyzed the NR3C2 gene in 14 families with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1 and found 6 heterozygous mutations. Two frameshift mutations in exon 2 (insT1354 and del8bp537) and a nonsense mutation in exon 4 (C645X) were predicted to produce truncated proteins. Three missense mutations (G633R, Q776R, and L979P) affected receptor function in different ways. The authors suggested that L979P has a transdominant negative effect on wildtype receptor activity, whereas G633R and Q776R probably result in haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Riepe et al. (2006) found 6 heterozygous NR3C2 mutations in 6 patients with PHA1. These were 2 frameshift mutations (c.1131dupT, previously reported, and c.2871dupC), 2 novel nonsense mutations that produce a truncated receptor protein, and 2 missense mutations (S818L and E972G). Functional studies included aldosterone binding, transactivation, subcellular translocation, proteolysis experiments, and 3-dimensional modeling.

(1959) described 'pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism,' with renal sodium loss, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia due to renal tubular insensitivity to mineralocorticoids. Hanukoglu et al. (1978) addressed the inheritance of pseudohypoaldosteronism.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with sporadic PHA1, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift mutation, a 1-bp insertion (2871insC) in exon 9 of the NR3C2 gene. The mutation impaired the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain and was absent in the asymptomatic family members.

checks.claim: In a patient with sporadic PHA1, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift 1-bp insertion (2871insC) in exon 9 of the NR3C2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: In the sporadic case we identified a new frameshift mutation, Ins2871C, in exon 9 of the hMR gene.
checks.explanation: Ins2871C means one C was inserted, so it is a 1-bp insertion. hMR is NR3C2.

checks.claim: The NR3C2 2871insC mutation impaired the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.
checks.evidence_quote: This mutation is the first described in exon 9 and impairs the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.

checks.claim: The NR3C2 2871insC mutation was absent in the asymptomatic family members of the sporadic PHA1 patient.
checks.evidence_quote: Family members were asymptomatic and had no mutation.

paragraphs.text: Riepe et al. (2006) found that this mutation, which they designated c.2871dupC, abolished aldosterone binding and transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation.

checks.claim: Riepe et al. (2006) designated the NR3C2 2871insC mutation as c.2871dupC.
checks.evidence_quote: The second frameshift mutation (c.2871dupC), which has only recently been reported by our group,
checks.explanation: The authors call the mutation c.2871dupC. The link to the name 2871insC comes from elsewhere in the entry and is equivalent notation.

checks.claim: Riepe et al. (2006) found that the NR3C2 c.2871dupC mutation abolished aldosterone binding and transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation.
checks.evidence_quote: showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation.

paragraphs.text: Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous gly633-to-arg (G633R) mutation in the DNA-binding domain of NR3C2 in a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1. The mutant had reduced maximal transactivation, although its binding characteristics and ED50 of transactivation were comparable to wildtype. The authors suggested that the mutation probably causes haploinsufficiency.

checks.evidence_quote: Six heterozygous mutations were detected.
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms G633R is one of the heterozygous mutations found in this cohort. It does not say how many families carried it, so 'in a family' cannot be confirmed from the abstract.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with PHA1, Riepe et al. (2006) identified a heterozygous ser818-to-leu (S818L) mutation in the NR3C2 gene. The mutant receptor did not bind aldosterone, activate transcription, or translocate into the nucleus. Modeling showed a major displacement of several residues involved in aldosterone binding.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with PHA1, Riepe et al. (2006) identified a heterozygous glu972-to-gly (E972G) mutation in the NR3C2 gene. The mutant had significantly lower ligand-binding affinity and only 9% of wildtype transcriptional activity, which the authors attributed to major changes in receptor conformation.
